title: Lost to science for 126 years: Indigenous knowledge and camera trapping document the critically endangered Otidiphaps insularis (Black-naped Pheasant-Pigeon)
content:
Abstract
As the global biodiversity crisis unfolds, species that remain scientifically unobserved for extended periods present a conservation dilemma: Are they simply undocumented or extinct? Otidiphaps insularis (Black-Naped Pheasant-Pigeon) is a critically endangered terrestrial bird species endemic to Fergusson Island, Papua New Guinea, with just 3 known museum specimens that had not been documented by Western scientists for 126 years and was feared extinct. We bridged standard ornithological surveying techniques with knowledge held by Indigenous and local people on Fergusson to successfully document O. insularis. Our objectives were to interview hunters about their bird knowledge and ability to identify O. insularis, conduct targeted surveys with hunters who had recently observed it, and conduct visual and acoustic bird surveys and camera trap surveys to document O. insularis and Fergusson’s avian community in general. Hunters (n = 29) interviewed during the study had high bird identification accuracy. Eleven hunters (38%) identified O. insularis from visual cues, and 5 (17%) identified it from acoustic cues involving playback of its congeners. Two hunters (7%) reported observing O. insularis within ≤1 year and guided surveys leading to documenting the species on a camera trap in just 6 camera trap days. Bird surveys (n = 70) detected 97 bird species but not O. insularis, whereas camera traps along an elevational gradient operated for 235 camera days and detected 7 bird species, including a second capture of O. insularis. Interviewed participants shared cultural knowledge about O. insularis, including a name (auwo) in the local Galea language and its role in a legend, chants, and ceremonial use. The scarcity of observations over the course of a ∼1 month-long expedition and apparent lack of recent observations by most interviewed hunters, as well as ongoing threats from timber extraction and introduced alien species, support its current critically endangered Red List status. Our results provide an example of successful research bridging Indigenous and local knowledge with standard avian surveying techniques, which may be an effective strategy for surveying other cryptic, rare, or data-deficient species.
